resources.string: Every Compose screen starts with a composable function. Write one that shows a greeting with Text and call it from setContent.
Mark a composable with the Preview annotation to see it in Android Studio without starting the emulator. Add one preview for light theme and one for dark.
A Column places its children from top to bottom. Use verticalArrangement and horizontalAlignment to decide where they sit.
Line things up in a Row
A Row places its children side by side. Give one child a weight to let it take the space that is left.
A Box draws its children on top of each other. It is the easy way to put a label over a picture.
Modifiers set size, padding, background and click behavior. Their order matters: padding before a background is not the same as padding after it.
Load a drawable with painterResource and show it in an Image. Pick a contentScale such as Crop so the picture fills its frame.
Move every text the user sees to string resources and read it with stringResource. Your app becomes ready for translation.
A Button needs two things: an onClick lambda and some content, usually a Text. Start with one that changes what is on the screen.
Wrap a value in remember and mutableStateOf. When the value changes, Compose redraws only the parts that read it.
Move state up to the caller, then pass the value down and the events up. Stateless composables are easier to reuse and to test.
A TextField shows the value you give it and reports every change. Set keyboardOptions to open the number keyboard when you need digits.
A Switch fits a choice between on and off. Keep its checked value in state and update it in onCheckedChange.
A Card groups related content on its own surface. Use it for list items so each one reads as a single piece.
LazyColumn composes only the items that are visible, so long lists stay fast. Describe each row inside the items block.
LazyVerticalGrid lays items out in columns. Choose a fixed number of columns or let the grid adapt to the width of the screen.
Material 3 names colors by role: primary, secondary, tertiary, surface. Define them once in the theme and read them from MaterialTheme.colorScheme.
Create a second color scheme for dark mode and switch with isSystemInDarkTheme. Dark surfaces are easier on the eyes at night.
Put font files in res/font, build a FontFamily and assign it in Typography. Two to four text styles are enough for most apps.
Shapes are part of the theme too. Set small, medium and large shapes once and components such as Card pick them up.
Scaffold gives you slots for a top app bar, the content and more. Pass its padding to your list so nothing hides under the bar.
An icon can replace a word when its meaning is clear. Put an Icon inside an IconButton for actions such as expand or favorite.
Add the animateContentSize modifier and a composable grows or shrinks smoothly when its content changes. No extra state is needed.
A spring animation feels natural because it follows physics. Change dampingRatio for the bounce and stiffness for the speed.
animateColorAsState moves from one color to another when its target changes. Use it to highlight the item the user opened.
Screen readers read the contentDescription of images and icons. Write one for everything that carries meaning and pass null for pure decoration.
Everything a user can tap should be at least 48 by 48 dp. IconButton does this for you, so prefer it to a bare clickable icon.
Small text needs a contrast ratio of at least 4.5 to 1 against its background, large text 3 to 1. Check both the light and the dark theme.
Write a Compose test that finds a node, clicks it and checks the result. Tests catch mistakes before your users do.
Take what you learned and build something that is yours: pick a topic, design a theme, add motion. This app is exactly that.
